text: x RFID belongs to a group of technologies referred to as Automatic Identification & Data Capture (AIDC). x AIDC methods automatically identify objects, collect data about them, & enter those data directly into com- puter systems with little or no human intervention. x RFID tags contain an integrated circuit & an antenna, which transmit data to the RFID reader (interrogator). x The reader then converts the radio waves to a more usable form of data. x Information collected from the tags is stored in a database & analysed. x RFID is like barcoding in that data from a tag is captured by a device that stores the data in a database. x RFID, however, has several advantages over systems that use barcode asset tracking software. x The most notable is that RFID tag data can be read outside the line-of-sight, whereas barcodes must be aligned with an optical scanner. Fuel Cell x A fuel cell uses electrochemical reactions to generate electrical energy. x A fuel cell requires a continuous input of fuel and an oxidizing agent in order to sustain the reaction. x Hydrogen is the most common fuel used. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 29 x They were initially used by NASA to power space capsules and satellites. Fuel Cell Mechanism x A fuel cell consists of a cathode, an anode, and an electrolyte. x The electrolyte enables the movement of the ions between the electrodes. x At the anode, catalyst causes the fuel to undergo oxidation and generates +ve charged ions and electrons. x The ions move from the anode to the cathode and the same time, the electrons flow from the anode to the cathode through an external circuit, producing direct current electricity. x At the cathode, another catalyst causes ions, electrons, and oxygen to react, forming water as by-product. x The reaction rate of this electrochemical reaction is quite low. x The reaction rate between the fuel and the oxidizing agent is quite low. x Catalysts such as platinum or palladium or gold are used speed up the reaction. Advantages of fuel cells x Fuel cells are more efficient than thermal power plants (thermal energy Î mechanical energy Î electrical energy) as there is direct conversion of chemical energy into electrical energy. x Hydrogen fuel is abundantly available. x The by-product of fuel cells are water and non-toxic products that pose no risk to our climate. Disadvantages of fuel cells x They are very expensive to produce (platinum, palladium catalysts are expensive). x As of now, there is no simple means of producing hydrogen fuel in a cost effective way. x Hydrogen itself is very prone to catching on fire, or even exploding. x In order to actually generate hydrogen fuel, fossil fuels are needed. Nuclear Fusion – International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER) PMF IAS – Learn Smart 30 x ITER is an international nuclear fusion research & engineering megaproject. x It was launched in 1985. x It is an experimental Tokamak Nuclear Fusion Reactor that is being built in southern France. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 31 x The ITER reactor has been designed to create a plasma of 500 megawatts for around twenty minutes on an input of 50 megawatts of thermal power (ten–fold gain of plasma heating power). x ITER will be the first fusion device to produce net energy. x Net Energy: When the total power produced during a fusion plasma pulse surpasses the thermal power injected to heat the plasma. ITER Members x China, the EU, India, Japan, Korea, Russia and the United States (collaboration of 35 nations). x They are collaborating to build the world's largest tokamak. x They are engaged in a 35-year collaboration to build and operate the ITER experimental device, and together bring fusion to the point where a demonstration fusion reactor can be designed. Tokamak x It is a magnetic fusion device that has been designed to prove the feasibility of fusion as a large-scale and carbon-free source of energy based on the same principle that powers our Sun and stars. HL-2M Tokamak x The HL-2M Tokamak reactor is China’s largest and most advanced nuclear fusion research device. x Scientists hope that the device can potentially unlock a powerful clean energy source. x It uses a powerful magnetic field to fuse hot plasma and to contain & control the hot plasma. x It can reach temperatures of over 150 million degrees Celsius — ten times hotter than the core of the sun. x Located in Sichuan province, the reactor is often called an “artificial sun” on account of the enormous heat and power it produces. India & ITER PMF IAS – Learn Smart 32 x India formally joined the ITER Project in 2005. x The ITER Agreement between the partners was signed in 2006. x ITER Organization (IO) is the central team responsible for site construction & operation. x ITER partners created their own domestic agencies to deliver their commitments to ITER. x ITER–India is the Indian domestic agency, a specially empowered project of the Institute for Plasma Re- search (IPR), an aided organization under Dept. of Atomic Energy. x ITER–India is responsible for delivery of the following ITER packages: 9 ITER India has shipped the base, upper cylinder & lower cylinder for the cryostat. 9 Cryostat is a cylindrical vessel which will act has a huge refrigerator & provide cooling to the fusion reactor that will attempt to harness the energy produced by fusion of atoms. Nuclear Fission vs. Nuclear Fusion x Nuclear Fusion and Nuclear Fission are different types of reactions that release energy due to the presence of high-powered atomic bonds between particles found within a nucleus. x In fission, an atom is split into two or more smaller, lighter atoms. x In fusion, two or more smaller atoms fuse together, creating a larger, heavier atom. Nuclear Fission Nuclear Fusion Definition x Fission is the splitting of a large atom into two or more smaller ones. x Fusion is the fusing of two or more lighter atoms into a larger one. Natural oc- currence of the process x Fission reaction does not normally occur in nature. x Fusion occurs in stars, such as the sun. By-products of the reac- tion x Fission produces many highly radi- oactive particles (nuclear waste). x Few radioactive particles are produced by fu- sion reaction, but if a fission "trigger" is used, ra- dioactive particles will result from that. Conditions x Critical mass of the substance and high-speed neutrons are required. x High density, high temperature environment is required. Energy Re- quirement x Takes little energy to split two at- oms in a fission reaction. x Extremely high energy is required to bring two or more protons close enough that nu- clear forces overcome their electrostatic PMF IAS – Learn Smart 34 repulsion. (This is what makes developing a Nu- clear Fusion Reactor so challenging) Energy Re- leased x The energy released by fission is a million times greater than that re- leased in chemical reactions, but lower than the energy released by nuclear fusion. x The energy released by fusion is three to four times greater than the energy released by fis- sion. Nuclear weapon x One class of nuclear weapon is a fission bomb, also known as an atomic bomb or atom bomb. x One class of nuclear weapon is the hydrogen bomb, which uses a fission reaction to "trigger" a fusion reaction. Energy pro- duction x Fission is used in nuclear power plants. x Fusion is an experimental technology for pro- ducing power. Fuel x Uranium is the primary fuel used in power plants. x Hydrogen isotopes (Deuterium and Tritium) are the primary fuel used in experimental fusion power plants. Reactions x It involves a chain reaction, which can lead to dangerous meltdowns x There is no chain reaction involved. Waste x Nuclear waste, a by-product of fission, is an environmental chal- lenge. x There is no nuclear waste. Lithium-ion battery, Lithium, Cobalt, EVs vs. ICEVs Lithium-ion battery PMF IAS – Learn Smart 35 Schematic of a rechargeable battery (Image Credits) x Anode, cathode, electrolyte and separator are the main components of a lithium ion (rechargeable) battery. x The two electrodes are immersed in the electrolyte and are separated by the separator. x The anode is usually made up of graphite (carbon). x Carbon graphite has a layered structure that can store the lithium ions in between its layers. x The cathode is made up of a combination of lithium-cobalt. x Lithium is unstable in the element form; hence the combination lithium-cobalt oxide is used for cathode. x Cathode plays an important role in determining the energy density of a Li-ion battery. x The higher amount of lithium, bigger the capacity. Working of a typical lithium-ion battery x Both electrodes in a li-ion battery can intercalate or ‘absorb’ lithium ions. x When the battery is being charged, lithium ions are absorbed (stored) in the anode. x During discharge, lithium ions naturally flow back to the cathode through the electrolyte. x This creates free electrons in the anode which move along the wire generating electricity. x The process (to and fro movement of lithium ion) repeats with each charge and discharge cycles. x Charge Process: Positive electrode (cathode) is oxidized (loses electrons) and Li+ ions pass across the electrolyte and are intercalated (insert between layers) in negative electrode (anode – graphite). x Discharge Process (opposite of charge process): An oxidation reaction occurs at the anode (-ve), Li+ ions are de-intercalated and migrate across the electrolyte to be re-intercalated into the cathode material. x Electrolyte (lithium salt) enables the movement of lithium ions between the electrodes. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 36 x The separator functions as a physical barrier keeping cathode and anode apart. x It prevents the direct flow of electrons and lets only the ions pass through. x While the cathode determines the performance of a battery, electrolyte and separator determines its safety. x Permeable polymer membranes such as polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP) are used as separators. Why lithium? x Lithium is the lightest metal and a powerful reducing agent (willing to donate its electrons). x Lithium ion batteries capitalize on the strong reducing potential of lithium ions to power the redox reaction — reduction at the cathode, oxidation at the anode. Role of cobalt in Lithium ion batteries x Lithium-cobalt-oxide is used as cathode in rechargeable batteries. x Lithium-cobalt-oxide is an intercalation compound with the lithium, cobalt and oxygen arranged in layers. x Cobalt is indispensable to assure the rate performance (rate of charging & discharging occurs). x When the lithium ion arrives or departs from cathode, cobalt changes its oxidation state (compensates for the gain/loss of charge) so that the lithium-cobalt-oxide stays electrically neutral. x Cathodes are commonly oxides made from transition metals such as nickel, cobalt, copper, iron, etc. x Replacing the costly cobalt with significantly cheaper nickel can be a fire hazard. x Aluminium & manganese can be added to stabilize, but it lowers the capacity of the cell by a small amount.
